posts.title: Fourteen coils before the van was loaded
posts.excerpt: Brightwell Electrical collected fourteen coils across two early mornings while rewiring a 1960s terrace.
posts.content:
Brightwell Electrical is a two-person domestic firm. The job was a rewire of a 1960s terrace, and the cable for it came off the counter at Kairo Supply in fourteen coils, collected over two early mornings. That is the whole of the story as the counter records it, and it is enough to show what the early shift is for.

The counter is Unit 4, Northgate Trade Park, 18 Mill Lane, Northbridge. On weekdays it opens at 06:30. Daniel Osei leads that shift, and he has done so since 2011. His line for the morning is plain: by ten to seven the first vans are loaded, and most of what they take was picked the evening before. A two-person firm rewiring a terrace does not have a store of its own. The coils have to be on the counter before the van is loaded, or the morning on site starts late.

Picking follows the clock. Phone or e-mail the order before 17:00 and it is picked for 06:30. The number is +00 0000 4710 and the mailbox is counter@kairo-supply.example. An order placed by 14:00 is on the counter the same day, if the firm is collecting in person later that afternoon. An order placed by 17:00 is delivered the next morning. Brightwell's two collections were early ones, which sits with the 06:30 opening rather than with an afternoon call. Saturday is shorter, 07:30 to 12:00, and the counter is closed on Sunday and on public holidays.

The cable they took sits, with everyone else's, on 180 drums. Tomás Herrera cuts it to length while you wait. A cut is €4, and it is free from 10 m. Fourteen coils is a lot of bench work for a two-person firm, and it is ordinary work for the drum yard. A drum that leaves the yard is a different matter: the deposit is €45, refunded when the drum is returned. Coils cut at the counter do not require that deposit. The shelves around the bench hold 4,200 lines, so a gland or a breaker can go on the same docket as the last ten metres of cable. Lena Vogt looks after the fittings and the distribution boards if a terrace rewire needs them on the same morning.

A firm of this size opens a trade account in the same three stages as any other. Apply, in about ten minutes, at the counter or by e-mail, with the company registration and one trade reference. The credit decision comes within two working days. The account number arrives by e-mail, with an opening limit of €2,500 and terms of 30 days from the end of the month. Opening the account is €0. Up to five named people can hold cards, each with a PIN, which for a two-person firm is more than the van needs, and the spare names can stay unused. The limit is reviewed after three months. Statements go monthly by e-mail. Priya Raman runs that desk. The story of the terrace does not turn on the paperwork, but the paperwork is what lets the second early collection happen without the firm introducing itself again.

If the coils had been wanted before the counter opened, the other route is the lockers. Collection from them runs from 17:00 to 06:30, the charge is €0, and a PIN arrives by text message. Samuel Adeyemi looks after the lockers and the van. Brightwell's collections are described as early collections, not as locker collections, so the counter desk is the faithful reading. The locker remains there for a morning that starts even earlier than 06:30.

The other firms on the same counter show the same clock from different trades. Halden Solar takes roof cable and isolators next morning for three installs a week. Next-morning delivery before 08:00 is €28, and a van within 25 km is €18, free over €400 net. Northfield Facilities, a hospital maintenance team, runs one account with five card holders and a monthly statement. Meridian Panels, a panel builder, had cable cut to thirty-seven exact lengths from a single drum. None of those jobs is the terrace. They are the reason the shelves, the drums and the account are not set up for domestic work alone.

Kairo Supply has been a family counter since 1987, run now by the second generation after a son and daughter took over in 2015. Marta Kovač has managed the branch since she joined in 2004. The line the branch uses for itself is stock, not promises. Fourteen coils for a 1960s terrace is what that looks like on a weekday before seven: the cable already cut, the docket in the firm's name, the van loaded, and the counter still open until 17:00 for whoever comes in next.
